## Learning goals

Chapter 15 showed what dynamic stochastic general equilibrium (DSGE) models say about business cycles. This
appendix opens the machine. With **Snowdrop**, a free Python package written at the International Monetary Fund
(Goumilevski and Otterson, 2025), you will write, solve, simulate and estimate DSGE models yourself. By the end of
this appendix you will be able to:

- explain what makes a model *dynamic*, *stochastic* and *general equilibrium*, and what it means to **solve** and
  to **estimate** one;
- solve a model with **rational expectations** by hand, and say why it needs the **Blanchard–Kahn** condition;
- read and write a Snowdrop **model file**, and simulate three models with it: the AS/AD model of Chapter 13, the
  monetary policy model of the Snowdrop paper, and a real business cycle model;
- read **impulse responses** and **contribution charts**, and check that a numerical solution is right;
- explain how the **Kalman filter** turns a model into a likelihood, and estimate a parameter by **maximum
  likelihood** with a few lines of NumPy;
- estimate Ireland's (2004) New Keynesian model on U.S. data by maximum likelihood and by **Bayesian posterior
  mode**, and judge how much the **priors** matter.

The appendix assumes Chapters 12, 13 and 15 and Appendices A and C. Everything else is explained as it comes.

## G.1 What a DSGE model is, and what estimating one means

Each word of the name says something about the model.

- **Dynamic.** Decisions link the periods. Households save today to consume tomorrow, firms invest today to produce
  tomorrow, and what people *expect* about the future changes what they do today.
- **Stochastic.** Random shocks hit the economy: to productivity, to preferences, to the costs of firms, to monetary
  policy. The shocks are what make the economy fluctuate; without them it would sit in its steady state.
- **General equilibrium.** All markets clear at once, and every household's and firm's plans are consistent with
  each other and with the resource constraint of the economy.

<!-- cell -->

### The ingredients

A DSGE model is a list of equations. Most of them come from one of five ingredients:

1. **Optimizing households and firms.** The Euler equation for consumption (Chapter 16), the demand for capital
   (Chapter 17) and price setting by firms are first-order conditions of optimization problems.
2. **Expectations.** Today's choices depend on what people expect tomorrow. DSGE models assume **rational
   expectations**: people's forecasts are the model's own forecasts, so they make no systematic mistakes.
3. **Constraints and market clearing.** Output is consumed or invested; the capital stock carries over from one
   period to the next.
4. **Shocks.** Each shock follows a simple random process, usually an AR(1): $z_t=\rho z_{t-1}+\varepsilon_t$.
5. **Policy rules.** The central bank follows a rule for the interest rate, like the rule of Chapter 13.

To **solve** the model is to find **decision rules**: formulas that give every variable today as a function of
the past (the *state* of the economy) and of today's shocks. With the decision rules we can simulate the economy
for any sequence of shocks.

<!-- cell -->

### From equations to numbers: the workflow

| Step | What happens | In this appendix |
|---|---|---|
| 1. Write | equations, variables, shocks and parameters go into a **model file** | G.5, G.6 |
| 2. Calibrate | choose parameter values from long-run facts and other studies | G.6–G.8 |
| 3. Steady state | find the values that the model settles at when no shocks hit | G.8 |
| 4. Solve | find the decision rules (linear models) or the whole path (nonlinear models) | G.4, G.7, G.8 |
| 5. Simulate | impulse responses, scenarios, contribution charts | G.6–G.8 |
| 6. Take to data | write the solution in **state-space form**; the **Kalman filter** gives the likelihood | G.9–G.11 |
| 7. Estimate | choose the parameters that make the data most likely, with or without priors | G.10–G.12 |

<!-- cell -->

### Calibration versus estimation

There are two ways to choose the parameters. **Calibration**, the approach of the real business cycle school
(Chapter 15), takes each value from outside evidence: the capital share from the national accounts, the discount
factor from average interest rates. **Estimation** lets the model's own time series pick the values: the
parameters that make the observed data most likely win (**maximum likelihood**). **Bayesian estimation** combines
the two: outside evidence enters as a **prior** distribution for each parameter, and the data update it. Most
central banks estimate their DSGE models this way (Smets and Wouters, 2007; Del Negro et al., 2013).

<!-- cell -->

### The toolboxes

Economists rarely code solvers from scratch. Three toolboxes dominate: **Dynare** (free, runs on MATLAB or the free
Octave), **IRIS** (free, runs on MATLAB) and **TROLL** (commercial). MATLAB itself is commercial software. A
Python package removes the license cost and connects DSGE modeling to the data tools of Appendices A and B. That is
the gap Snowdrop wants to fill.

<!-- cell -->

## G.2 The Snowdrop paper

The paper is Goumilevski, A., and Otterson, J. (2025), "Snowdrop: Python Package for DSGE Modeling," *Journal of
Open Source Software* 10(112), 8197 ([doi:10.21105/joss.08197](https://doi.org/10.21105/joss.08197)). The code
is on GitHub at [gumilevskij/Framework](https://github.com/gumilevskij/Framework). Both authors work at the
International Monetary Fund. The *Journal of Open Source Software* (JOSS) publishes short papers about research
software: the paper is a summary, and the software itself goes through peer review (installation, documentation,
tests). The details are in the package's 56-page User Guide and its notes on numerical algorithms, which come with
the code.

<!-- cell -->

### Why Snowdrop exists

The paper's statement of need makes four points:

- DSGE models are a basic tool of central banks for monetary policy and forecasting (it cites work at the IMF, the
  ECB, the Federal Reserve Bank of New York and the Japanese Ministry of Finance).
- Python, for all its scientific libraries, lacked an integrated DSGE toolbox.
- Each existing toolbox has a strength: Dynare is easy to use but handles only **stationary** models, so users must
  rewrite growing variables as ratios; IRIS handles **non-stationary** models; TROLL solves very large systems. But
  all of them are commercial or run on commercial software.
- Snowdrop is free (GNU General Public License) and handles a wide range of models. Benchmarked against Dynare and
  IRIS on models with several hundred equations, it runs about as fast and needs less memory.

<!-- cell -->

### What the package does

| Feature | In Snowdrop | Where you meet it |
|---|---|---|
| Model files | human-readable YAML; also Python scripts, Dynare, IRIS and Sirius XML files | G.5–G.8, G.11 |
| Nonlinear models | perfect-foresight paths by **Newton's method**: the stacked **ABLR** method and the forward–backward **LBJ** method (Juillard et al., 1998) | G.4, G.7, G.8 |
| Linear models | Binder–Pesaran, Anderson–Moore, and two **generalized Schur** methods that reproduce Dynare and IRIS | G.8, G.11 |
| Time-varying parameters | a parameter can follow a path | G.5 |
| Estimation | maximum likelihood, and a **Bayesian** version with priors | G.11, G.12 |
| Sampling | Markov chain Monte Carlo: the **emcee** ensemble sampler of Goodman and Weare, and adaptive Metropolis–Hastings | G.13 |
| Filters | Kalman (several versions), unscented Kalman, particle, Hodrick–Prescott, band-pass | G.9–G.11 |
| Output | plots, contribution charts, Excel and SQLite files | throughout |

It runs on Windows, macOS and Linux, on CPUs and, through the CuPy library, on GPUs.

<!-- cell -->

### The paper's three examples

1. **A monetary policy model** with four equations: a Phillips curve, a real interest rate, a policy rule and an
   IS curve. The paper prints its model file and, in its Fig. 1, the forecast of inflation, the real and nominal
   interest rates and the output gap after a 2 percent output shock in period 1 and a 3 percentage point revision
   of the policy rate in period 4, split into the contribution of each term. **Section G.7 replicates Fig. 1.**
2. **Ireland's (2004) New Keynesian model**, estimated on U.S. data. **Sections G.11 and G.12 estimate it.**
3. **The Eichenbaum–Rebelo–Trabandt (2020) model** of the macroeconomics of epidemics, with two strains of a virus,
   sticky- and flexible-price economies linked by a Taylor rule, and 64 equations. It is highly nonlinear, and
   Snowdrop solves it by a *homotopy*: it moves the parameters step by step from an easy case to the real one. The
   paper's Figs. 2 and 3 forecast infections, deaths and the economy for 2020–2022. This model is too big for an
   introduction; Section G.13 tells you where its files are.

<!-- cell -->

### How the paper runs a model

The paper gives three steps: write or edit a YAML model file, open the test script `tests/test_toy_models.py` and
set `fname` to the file's name, then run the script. In a notebook we do the same with two functions:
`importModel` reads the file, and `run` solves and simulates the model.

<!-- cell -->

### Reading research software with care

A short paper cannot document everything, and research code changes faster than its documentation. As we go, we
will meet a few places where the paper, the User Guide and the code disagree, or where a function needs help. None
of them is serious, but each one teaches the habit that matters most in computational economics: **check every
result**. Compare it with a case you can solve by hand, look at the residuals of the equations, and try more than
one starting point. The appendix shows how.

## G.3 Setup

<!-- cell -->

### Installing Snowdrop

Snowdrop is not part of Colab, so we install it. One detail matters. The package asks for old versions of NumPy
(1.26) and SciPy (1.11), which do not exist for Colab's Python 3.13: a plain install would fail. Everything this
appendix uses runs on Colab's own, newer NumPy and SciPy, so we install Snowdrop **without its version
requirements** (`--no-deps`), together with the three small libraries it needs and Colab lacks: `particles`
(probability distributions), `ruamel.yaml` (it reads YAML files; Snowdrop needs version 0.17.21) and that
library's C helper. We install a fixed version of Snowdrop: the GitHub commit of 3 October 2026, which corrected
the standard errors of estimated parameters. The install takes about 20 seconds. pip then prints a note that you
may need to restart the kernel; you do not, because the install changes nothing that Colab has already loaded.

> **Python note.** `%pip install` is a notebook command, not Python: it installs packages into the computer that
> runs the notebook. `-q` keeps it quiet, and `--no-deps` installs exactly the packages named, nothing else. A
> GitHub address ending in `.tar.gz` is a compressed copy of the code at one commit.

```{python}
# Snowdrop at the commit of 3 October 2026, without its old NumPy/SciPy pins, plus three small libraries
%pip install -q --no-deps "https://github.com/gumilevskij/Framework/archive/47a63b2b780e1876898229c09f7f1e8644462692.tar.gz"
%pip install -q --no-deps particles==0.4 "ruamel.yaml==0.17.21" ruamel.yaml.clib
```

<!-- cell -->

### Libraries and the work folder

Snowdrop writes files next to each model file it reads (a cache of the parsed model) and into an output folder. We
keep all of that in one work folder, `dsge`. Two lines need a word of explanation. Snowdrop first tries the GPU
library CuPy; we tell Python that CuPy is not available, so Snowdrop always uses the CPU. And importing Snowdrop
moves Python into Snowdrop's own folder, so we move back to ours right after.

```{python}
# Libraries used in this appendix
import os, sys, io, re, shutil, contextlib
import numpy as np                          # numbers and arrays
import pandas as pd                         # data tables
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt             # Snowdrop's charts, and ours
from scipy import optimize, stats           # numerical solvers and probability distributions
from IPython.display import HTML, display

sys.modules["cupy"] = None                  # no GPU library: Snowdrop uses the CPU
WORK = os.path.abspath("dsge")              # our work folder: model files, data, Snowdrop's output
os.makedirs(WORK, exist_ok=True)
os.environ["PLATFORM_OUTPUT_FOLDER"] = os.path.join(WORK, "output")

import snowdrop.src                         # importing Snowdrop moves Python into its own folder ...
from snowdrop.src import driver             # driver: importModel, run, estimate, ...
from snowdrop.src.graphs.util import plot, plotDecomposition
os.chdir(WORK)                              # ... so we move back to ours
print("Working in:", os.getcwd())
```

<!-- cell -->

Snowdrop comes with example models and data. We copy the files we need into the work folder, so that Snowdrop's
cache files land there too.

```{python}
SUPP = os.path.join(os.path.dirname(snowdrop.src.__file__), "..", "..", "supplements")
SUPP = os.path.abspath(SUPP)                # Snowdrop's example models and data
print("Example models:", sorted(os.listdir(os.path.join(SUPP, "models", "TOY"))))

for name in ["JLMP98.yaml", "RBC.yaml", "RBC1.yaml", "Ireland2004.yaml"]:
    shutil.copy(os.path.join(SUPP, "models", "TOY", name), WORK)
shutil.copy(os.path.join(SUPP, "data", "gpr_1948.csv"), WORK)
print("Copied to the work folder:", sorted(os.listdir(WORK)))
```

### The book's chart style, in light and dark

Snowdrop draws its charts with matplotlib. The four helper cells below give every chart of this appendix,
Snowdrop's and ours, the colors of the book, and save each chart twice: a light version (Colab, and the website's
light theme) and a dark version (the website's dark theme). You do not need to read them. You only use four
functions:

- `show(fig, "a description")` shows a chart; add `snowdrop=True` for a chart that Snowdrop drew;
- `load_model(file)` reads a model file quietly (`load_model(file, verbose=True)` prints Snowdrop's report);
- `simulate(model)` solves and simulates a model quietly and returns a table;
- `set_values(model, "parameters", {...})` changes values in a model.

```{python}
#| kind: helper
# @title Helper code: the book's colors, and their versions for the dark theme
import math, base64, matplotlib, matplotlib.collections, matplotlib.patches
from matplotlib.colors import to_rgba, to_hex
BLUE, TEAL, GREEN, GRAY, ORANGE, RUST = "#16528c", "#008070", "#7fb23a", "#8a96a3", "#e0a33b", "#c4651a"
SERIES = [BLUE, "#5aa0d8", TEAL, GREEN, ORANGE, "#b04a5a", "#8e5ea2", GRAY, RUST, "#0b4f47"]
INK, GRID, AXIS, TOTAL, NAVY = "#2a3f5f", "#e3e9f1", "#b8c4d2", "#1b2733", "#06253e"
DARK = {"#16528c": "#5eb1f2", "#008070": "#3dd6c4", "#7fb23a": "#a6d85b", "#8a96a3": "#97a9bd",
        "#5aa0d8": "#a9d3f7", "#0b4f47": "#22a08d", "#e0a33b": "#f2c14e", "#c4651a": "#f08c4a",
        "#b04a5a": "#f07a8c", "#8e5ea2": "#c39be0", INK: "#d8e3ee", TOTAL: "#e6edf5",
        "#000000": "#e6edf5", "#ffffff": NAVY}

def _lin(v): return v / 12.92 if v <= 0.04045 else ((v + 0.055) / 1.055) ** 2.4
def _gam(v): return min(1.0, max(0.0, 12.92 * v if v <= 0.0031308 else 1.055 * v ** (1 / 2.4) - 0.055))
def oklab(rgb):
    r, g, b = (_lin(x) for x in rgb[:3])
    l, m, s = [(u * r + v * g + w * b) ** (1 / 3) for u, v, w in ((0.4122214708, 0.5363325363, 0.0514459929),
               (0.2119034982, 0.6806995451, 0.1073969566), (0.0883024619, 0.2817188376, 0.6299787005))]
    return (0.2104542553 * l + 0.7936177850 * m - 0.0040720468 * s,
            1.9779984951 * l - 2.4285922050 * m + 0.4505937099 * s,
            0.0259040371 * l + 0.7827717662 * m - 0.8086757660 * s)
def from_oklab(L, A, B):
    for k in np.arange(1.0, -0.01, -0.05):                     # lower the chroma until the color fits sRGB
        a, b = A * k, B * k
        l, m, s = (L + 0.3963377774 * a + 0.2158037573 * b) ** 3, (L - 0.1055613458 * a - 0.0638541728 * b) ** 3, \
                  (L - 0.0894841775 * a - 1.2914855480 * b) ** 3
        rgb = (4.0767416621 * l - 3.3077115913 * m + 0.2309699292 * s, -1.2684380046 * l + 2.6097574011 * m
               - 0.3413193965 * s, -0.0041960863 * l - 0.7034186147 * m + 1.7076147010 * s)
        if k < 0.05 or all(-0.002 < v < 1.002 for v in rgb):
            return tuple(_gam(v) for v in rgb)
NAVY_LAB = oklab(to_rgba(NAVY))
def dark_color(c, role="ink"):
    """The dark-theme version of a color: the same rules as the website's Plotly charts."""
    r, g, b, a = to_rgba(c)
    if a == 0:
        return (r, g, b, a)
    L, A, B = oklab((r, g, b)); chroma = math.hypot(A, B); hexc = to_hex((r, g, b))
    if role == "rule" and chroma >= 0.035: role = "ink"
    if role == "ink" and hexc in DARK:
        return to_rgba(DARK[hexc], a * 0.85 if a < 1 else 1)
    if chroma < 0.035 or (role != "ink" and L > 0.6):          # neutrals: swap light and dark
        hi, lo = (0.78 if role == "rule" else 0.93), (NAVY_LAB[0] + 0.08 if role == "ink" and L < 0.985 else NAVY_LAB[0])
        L2 = hi - (hi - lo) * L; f = max(0.0, (1 - L2) / (1 - NAVY_LAB[0]))
        A, B = A * 0.6 + NAVY_LAB[1] * f, B * 0.6 + NAVY_LAB[2] * f
    else:
        L2 = 0.66 + L * 0.175 if (role == "ink" and L < 0.8) else L   # lift dark ink above the navy
    return (*from_oklab(L2, A, B), a * 0.85 if (role == "ink" and a < 1) else a)
```

```{python}
#| kind: helper
# @title Helper code: restyle a chart (Snowdrop's colors to the book's; light to dark)
def recolor(fig, fn):
    """Apply fn(color, role) to every color of a matplotlib figure; role is paper, rule or ink."""
    fig.patch.set_facecolor(fn(fig.patch.get_facecolor(), "paper"))
    for t in fig.texts: t.set_color(fn(t.get_color(), "ink"))
    for ax in fig.axes:
        ax.set_facecolor(fn(ax.get_facecolor(), "paper"))
        for sp in ax.spines.values(): sp.set_edgecolor(fn(sp.get_edgecolor(), "rule"))
        for axis in (ax.xaxis, ax.yaxis):
            for gl in axis.get_gridlines(): gl.set_color(fn(gl.get_color(), "rule"))
            for lab in axis.get_ticklabels(which="both"): lab.set_color(fn(lab.get_color(), "ink"))
            axis.label.set_color(fn(axis.label.get_color(), "ink"))
            axis.set_tick_params(which="both", color=fn(AXIS, "rule"))
        for t in [ax.title, ax._left_title, ax._right_title] + ax.texts: t.set_color(fn(t.get_color(), "ink"))
        for ln in ax.lines:
            role = "rule" if ln.get_gid() == "rule" else "ink"
            ln.set_color(fn(ln.get_color(), role))
            ln.set_markerfacecolor(fn(ln.get_markerfacecolor(), role)); ln.set_markeredgecolor(fn(ln.get_markeredgecolor(), role))
        for p in ax.patches:
            p.set_facecolor(fn(p.get_facecolor(), "ink")); p.set_edgecolor(fn(p.get_edgecolor(), "ink"))
        for col in ax.collections:
            col.set_facecolors([fn(c, "ink") for c in col.get_facecolors()])
            col.set_edgecolors([fn(c, "ink") for c in col.get_edgecolors()])
        leg = ax.get_legend()
        if leg is not None:
            leg.get_frame().set_facecolor(fn(leg.get_frame().get_facecolor(), "paper"))
            leg.get_frame().set_edgecolor(fn(leg.get_frame().get_edgecolor(), "rule"))
            for t in leg.get_texts(): t.set_color(fn(t.get_color(), "ink"))
            for h in leg.legend_handles:
                if isinstance(h, matplotlib.lines.Line2D):
                    h.set_color(fn(h.get_color(), "ink"))
                    h.set_markerfacecolor(fn(h.get_markerfacecolor(), "ink")); h.set_markeredgecolor(fn(h.get_markeredgecolor(), "ink"))
                elif isinstance(h, matplotlib.collections.Collection):
                    h.set_facecolors([fn(c, "ink") for c in h.get_facecolors()])
                    h.set_edgecolors([fn(c, "ink") for c in h.get_edgecolors()])
                elif isinstance(h, matplotlib.patches.Patch):
                    h.set_facecolor(fn(h.get_facecolor(), "ink")); h.set_edgecolor(fn(h.get_edgecolor(), "ink"))

```

```{python}
#| kind: helper
# @title Helper code: Snowdrop's colors to the book's colors
def to_book_colors(fig):
    """Snowdrop's colors -> the book's: black lines stay dark, red data dots become rust, others follow SERIES."""
    seen = {}
    def book(c, role):
        r, g, b, a = to_rgba(c); L, A, B = oklab((r, g, b)); chroma = math.hypot(A, B)
        if role == "paper": return to_rgba("white")
        if role == "rule": return to_rgba(GRID if L > 0.7 else AXIS)
        if chroma < 0.035: return to_rgba(TOTAL if L < 0.3 else (INK if L < 0.6 else "white"), a)
        if r > 0.9 and g < 0.15 and b < 0.15: return to_rgba(RUST, a)
        key = to_hex((r, g, b))
        if key not in seen: seen[key] = SERIES[len(seen) % len(SERIES)]
        return to_rgba(seen[key], a)
    recolor(fig, book)
    for ax in fig.axes:
        ax.grid(True, color=GRID, linewidth=0.8); ax.set_axisbelow(True)
        for p in ax.patches: p.set_edgecolor("white"); p.set_linewidth(0.6)
        leg = ax.get_legend()
        if leg is not None:
            for h in leg.legend_handles:
                if isinstance(h, matplotlib.patches.Patch): h.set_edgecolor("white")
```

```{python}
#| kind: helper
# @title Helper code: draw a chart in the book's style, and show it in both themes
BOOK_RC = {"figure.facecolor": "white", "axes.facecolor": "white", "axes.edgecolor": AXIS, "axes.labelcolor": INK,
           "axes.grid": True, "grid.color": GRID, "grid.linewidth": 0.8, "axes.spines.top": False,
           "axes.spines.right": False, "xtick.color": INK, "ytick.color": INK, "text.color": INK,
           "axes.titlesize": 13, "axes.titleweight": "normal", "axes.labelsize": 11, "legend.frameon": False,
           "axes.prop_cycle": matplotlib.cycler(color=SERIES), "lines.linewidth": 2.2, "font.size": 11}

def book_figure(rows=1, cols=1, width=8.6, height=4.6):
    """A new matplotlib figure in the book's style (Snowdrop's plots change the global style, so reset it)."""
    plt.rcdefaults(); plt.rcParams.update(BOOK_RC)
    fig, axes = plt.subplots(rows, cols, figsize=(width, height), squeeze=False)
    return fig, (axes[0, 0] if rows * cols == 1 else axes.ravel())

def _png(fig):
    buf = io.BytesIO()
    fig.savefig(buf, format="png", dpi=110, facecolor=fig.get_facecolor(), bbox_inches="tight")
    return base64.b64encode(buf.getvalue()).decode()

def show(fig, alt, snowdrop=False):
    """Show a chart twice, light and dark; the website picks the one that matches its theme."""
    if snowdrop:
        to_book_colors(fig)
    light = _png(fig)
    recolor(fig, dark_color)
    dark = _png(fig)
    plt.close(fig)
    alt = alt.replace('"', "'")
    display(HTML(f'<div class="book-mpl"><img class="book-mpl-light" alt="{alt}" src="data:image/png;base64,{light}">'
                 f'<img class="book-mpl-dark" alt="{alt}" style="display:none" src="data:image/png;base64,{dark}"></div>'))
```

```{python}
#| kind: helper
# @title Helper code: run Snowdrop quietly, change model values, read its estimation tables
import snowdrop.src.numeric.estimation.estimate as sd_estimate
os.chdir(WORK)                                    # this import also moves Python into Snowdrop's folder
ANSI = re.compile(r"\x1b\[[0-9;]*m")              # Snowdrop prints colored text; we strip the colors

def quietly(function, *args, **kwargs):
    """Call a Snowdrop function and keep its printout; return (result, text)."""
    buf = io.StringIO()
    with contextlib.redirect_stdout(buf):
        result = function(*args, **kwargs)
    return result, ANSI.sub("", buf.getvalue())

def load_model(file, verbose=False, **options):
    """Read a model file with importModel; print Snowdrop's report only if verbose."""
    model, text = quietly(driver.importModel, fname=os.path.join(WORK, file), **options)
    if verbose:
        print(text.strip())
    return model

def simulate(model, **options):
    """Solve and simulate a model with run(); return a table, one row per period, one column per variable."""
    (y, dates), text = quietly(driver.run, model=model, Plot=False, **options)
    y = np.asarray(y)
    return pd.DataFrame(y[:len(dates)], index=dates, columns=model.symbols["variables"])

def set_values(model, kind, values):
    """Change parameters or starting values: kind is 'parameters' or 'variables', values a dict name -> number."""
    names = model.symbols[kind]
    new = np.array(model.calibration[kind], dtype=float)  # Snowdrop's arrays are read-only: change a copy
    for name, value in values.items():
        new[names.index(name)] = value
    model.calibration[kind] = new

def estimate(model, **options):
    """Run Snowdrop's estimate() quietly; print its results table and return it as a DataFrame, with the output."""
    sd_estimate.est_shocks_names.clear()          # Snowdrop keeps a list here between runs; start afresh
    out, text = quietly(driver.estimate, model=model, Output=False, Plot=False, **options)
    start = text.find("Estimation\n+")
    print(text[text.rfind("\n", 0, start - 30) + 1: text.find("Estimation time")].strip())
    rows = re.findall(r"\|\s*(\w+)\s*\|\s*([-0-9.e]+)\s*\|\s*([-0-9.e]+)\s*\|\s*([-0-9.e]+)\s*\|", text)
    table = pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["parameter", "start", "estimate", "std. error"]).set_index("parameter")
    table = table.astype(float)
    table.attrs["log value"] = float(re.findall(r"function value: ([-0-9.]+)", text)[-1])
    return table, out
```

<!-- cell -->

## G.4 Rational expectations from small pieces

Before Snowdrop does it for us, let us solve the smallest possible model with expectations by hand. It shows what
"solving a DSGE model" means, and why a solution exists and is unique.

<!-- cell -->

### A model with one equation

Take the New Keynesian Phillips curve of Ireland's model in Section G.11, stripped to its core:

$$x_t = a\,\mathbb{E}_t[x_{t+1}] + b\,z_t, \qquad (G.1)$$

$$z_t = \rho\, z_{t-1} + \varepsilon_t. \qquad (G.2)$$

Read $x_t$ as inflation and $z_t$ as a cost shock that fades at rate $\rho$. Inflation today depends on the shock
today and on the inflation that people **expect** for tomorrow; $a$ is close to 1 (it is the discount factor of
price setters), and $b$ is the slope of the curve. The problem is that tomorrow's inflation depends on the day
after, and so on forever: today's inflation depends on all expected future shocks.

**Guess and verify.** Since only $z_t$ moves the economy, guess that inflation is proportional to it:
$x_t=\phi\,z_t$. Then $\mathbb{E}_t[x_{t+1}]=\phi\,\mathbb{E}_t[z_{t+1}]=\phi\rho z_t$, and equation (G.1) becomes
$\phi z_t = a\phi\rho z_t + b z_t$. This holds for every $z_t$ only if

$$\phi = \frac{b}{1-a\rho}. \qquad (G.3)$$

The guess works, and (G.3) is the **decision rule**. A shock that lasts longer (larger $\rho$) moves inflation
more, because price setters expect it to raise their costs for longer.

<!-- cell -->

We use teaching values: $a=0.9$, $b=0.14$ and $\rho=0.8$, so that $\phi=0.5$. A shock of 1 hits in period 1, and
after that the economy is left alone. With no more shocks, the expectation of tomorrow is simply tomorrow, so we
can check (G.1) period by period.

```{python}
a, b, rho = 0.9, 0.14, 0.8           # discount factor, slope, persistence of the cost shock
phi = b / (1 - a * rho)              # equation (G.3)
T = 30
z = np.zeros(T + 1)                  # periods 0, 1, ..., 30
z[1] = 1.0                           # a cost shock of 1 in period 1
for t in range(2, T + 1):
    z[t] = rho * z[t - 1]            # equation (G.2) with no new shocks
x = phi * z                          # the decision rule

residual = x[1:T] - a * x[2:T + 1] - b * z[1:T]  # equation (G.1), period by period
print(f"phi = b / (1 - a rho) = {phi:.3f}")
print(f"largest error in equation (G.1): {np.abs(residual).max():.1e}")
```

<!-- cell -->

```{python}
fig, ax = book_figure()
ax.plot(range(T + 1), z, color=GRAY, linestyle="--", label="cost shock $z_t$")
ax.plot(range(T + 1), x, color=BLUE, marker="o", markersize=4, label="inflation $x_t = \\phi z_t$")
ax.set_title("A cost shock and the inflation it causes")
ax.set_xticks(range(0, T + 1, 5))
ax.set_xlabel("period")
ax.legend()
show(fig, "Inflation follows the cost shock at half its size and fades at the same rate")
```

**What to notice.** Inflation jumps in period 1 and then fades at the rate of the shock, always at half its size
($\phi=0.5$). Nothing else moves inflation: the decision rule has turned a forward-looking equation into a simple
formula.

<!-- cell -->

### Why the solution is unique: stable and unstable paths

The decision rule is not the only path that satisfies (G.1) each period. Write the equation forward:
$x_{t+1}=(x_t-b\,z_t)/a$. Suppose inflation starts a little off the rule, by a gap $d_1=x_1-\phi z_1$. Subtracting
the rule from both sides gives

$$d_{t+1} = \frac{1}{a}\,d_t. \qquad (G.4)$$

Because $a<1$, the factor $1/a$ is larger than 1: any gap **explodes**. Of all the paths that satisfy (G.1), only
the one with no gap stays bounded. Inflation is a **jump variable**: nothing ties it to the past, so it jumps in
period 1 to the one value that keeps the economy on the stable path. This is the **Blanchard–Kahn condition** in its
simplest form. A linear model has a unique stable solution when the number of unstable roots (here $1/a>1$) equals
the number of jump variables (here one: $x_t$). Snowdrop counts both for every model it solves (Section G.5).

```{python}
fig, ax = book_figure()
gaps = [-0.1, -0.05, 0.0, 0.05, 0.1]          # how far inflation starts from the decision rule
for d in gaps:
    path = np.zeros(T + 1)
    path[1] = phi * z[1] + d
    for t in range(1, T):
        path[t + 1] = (path[t] - b * z[t]) / a  # equation (G.1) solved for next period's inflation
    if d == 0:
        ax.plot(range(1, T + 1), path[1:], color=BLUE, linewidth=3, label="the decision rule (gap 0)")
    else:
        ax.plot(range(1, T + 1), path[1:], color=GRAY, linewidth=1.3)
ax.plot([], [], color=GRAY, linewidth=1.3, label="starting gaps of ±0.05 and ±0.1")
ax.set_ylim(-1.5, 2.0)
ax.set_title("Only one path stays bounded: every other path explodes")
ax.set_xticks(range(0, T + 1, 5))
ax.set_xlabel("period")
ax.set_ylabel("inflation $x_t$")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
show(fig, "Paths of inflation that start off the decision rule explode; only the rule stays bounded")
print(f"Unstable root 1/a = {1 / a:.3f} > 1, one jump variable: a unique stable solution.")
```

<!-- cell -->

### Perfect foresight: the whole path as one system of equations

There is a second way to solve the model, and it is the one Snowdrop uses for nonlinear models. Look at all the
periods at once. Equation (G.1) for periods $1, 2, \dots, T$ gives $T$ equations in the $T$ unknowns
$x_1,\dots,x_T$, if we add a **terminal condition**: far in the future the economy is back at its steady state,
$x_{T+1}=0$. Solve the $T$ equations together and you have the whole path.

**Newton's method** solves such systems. Start from a guess for the path, compute the *residuals* (how far each
equation is from holding), and correct the guess with the matrix of derivatives (the Jacobian $J$):
$x \leftarrow x - J^{-1}\,\text{residuals}(x)$. For a linear model one step is enough; a nonlinear model needs a
few. Snowdrop's ABLR method stacks all periods into one large sparse system like this one, and its LBJ method
solves the same system period by period, forward and then backward.

> **Python note.** `rho ** np.arange(80)` gives $1, \rho, \rho^2, \dots$: the shock in periods 1 to 80.
> `np.append(x[1:], 0.0)` shifts the path one period ahead and adds the terminal value $x_{T+1}=0$. `np.eye(T)` is the identity matrix and `np.eye(T, k=1)` has ones just above the diagonal, so
> `J @ x` gives $x_t - a\,x_{t+1}$ for every $t$. `np.linalg.solve(J, r)` computes $J^{-1}r$.

```{python}
T_long = 80                                     # a long horizon, so that x_81 = 0 does no harm
z_long = rho ** np.arange(T_long)               # the cost shock in periods 1, ..., 80

def residuals(x_path):
    """Equation (G.1) for t = 1, ..., 80, with the terminal condition x_81 = 0."""
    x_next = np.append(x_path[1:], 0.0)
    return x_path - a * x_next - b * z_long

J = np.eye(T_long) - a * np.eye(T_long, k=1)    # the Jacobian of the residuals
guess = np.zeros(T_long)                        # start from "nothing happens"
for step in range(1, 4):
    guess = guess - np.linalg.solve(J, residuals(guess))
    print(f"Newton step {step}: largest residual {np.abs(residuals(guess)).max():.1e}")

print(f"Largest gap to the decision rule in periods 1-{T}: {np.abs(guess[:T] - x[1:T + 1]).max():.1e}")
```

**What to notice.** Newton's method converges in one step, because the model is linear; the later steps change
nothing. Its path matches the decision rule. The terminal condition $x_{81}=0$ is slightly wrong (the rule gives
$0.5\times0.8^{80}$), but 80 periods later that error no longer matters. With a short horizon it would: this is
why Snowdrop simulates models over many periods.

<!-- cell -->

**Your turn.** Set $a=1.1$. What is the unstable root $1/a$ now? Run the cell with the five starting gaps again:
do the other paths still explode? What does this mean for the uniqueness of the solution?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

With $a=1.1$ the root is $1/a\approx 0.91<1$: there is no unstable root but still one jump variable, so the
Blanchard–Kahn condition fails. Every gap now *shrinks*, so every starting value of inflation gives a bounded path.
The model has many stable solutions (it is **indeterminate**): it cannot tell us what inflation will be.
Expectations alone can then move the economy (economists call these *sunspots*). In New Keynesian models, a central
bank that raises the interest rate by more than one for one with inflation (the Taylor principle of Chapter 13)
rules this out.

```python
a = 1.1
phi = b / (1 - a * rho)       # the decision rule changes too
print(f"1/a = {1 / a:.3f}, phi = {phi:.3f}")   # then rerun the cell that draws the five paths
```

Set `a = 0.9` and `phi = b / (1 - a * rho)` again before you go on.

</details>

## G.5 Anatomy of a Snowdrop model file

<!-- cell -->

### YAML in five minutes

Snowdrop's model files are written in **YAML**, a plain-text format for structured data. Four rules cover almost
everything:

- `key: value` pairs, one per line;
- nesting by **indentation with spaces** (never tabs);
- lists either in brackets, `[x, z]`, or one item per line starting with `- `;
- `#` starts a comment.

Python reads YAML into dictionaries and lists. Here is a tiny example:

```{python}
import yaml
text = """
name: A tiny example          # the model's name
symbols:
   variables: [x, z]
   parameters: [a, b, rho]
calibration:
   a: 0.9
   b: 0.14
"""
print(yaml.safe_load(text))
```

<!-- cell -->

### The blocks of a model file

Here is the model file of the paper's monetary policy model, as it comes with Snowdrop. (Its name, JLMP98, points to
Juillard, Laxton, McAdam and Pioro, 1998, the paper behind Snowdrop's LBJ method.)

```{python}
print(open("JLMP98.yaml").read())
```

<!-- cell -->

| Block | What it holds |
|---|---|
| `name` | a description of the model |
| `symbols` | the names of the **variables** (endogenous), the **exogenous** variables (paths given from outside), the **shocks** and the **parameters** |
| `equations` | one equation per line, `left side = right side`; one equation per endogenous variable |
| `calibration` | parameter values, and **starting values** of the variables |
| `labels` | readable names for charts, also for leads and lags such as `PDOT(-1)` |
| `options` | simulation settings: `T` (number of periods), `periods` (when shocks hit), `shock_values` (their sizes) |

Models that are estimated have four more blocks: `measurement_variables`, `measurement_shocks`,
`measurement_equations` and `estimated_parameters`. We meet them in Section G.11.

<!-- cell -->

### Timing, shocks and exogenous variables

- `PDOT(-1)` is last period's value (a **lag**), and `PDOT(+1)` (or `PDOT(1)`) is the value people expect for next
  period (a **lead**). An equation with a lead is forward-looking.
- **Shocks** are listed under `symbols: shocks`. `options: periods: [1]` and `shock_values: [0.02]` mean "in period
  1, the shocks take these values", in the order of the shock list: here the first shock, `ey`, equals 0.02. Values
  not given are zero.
- **Exogenous variables** follow a path set from outside, period by period (G.7 uses one for the policy-rate
  revision).
- A parameter can **change over time**: in `calibration`, `p_pdot1: [0.4, 0.5, 0.6]` would mean 0.4 in period 1,
  0.5 in period 2 and 0.6 from period 3 on.

<!-- cell -->

### From file to model object

`importModel` reads the file, checks its syntax, and writes Python functions for the equations and their
derivatives. Its report lists the equations; the number in front of each one is its **residual** at the starting
values. A residual of 0.000 means the starting values satisfy that equation, which is a quick check that you start
from a steady state.

```{python}
jlmp = load_model("JLMP98.yaml", verbose=True)
```

<!-- cell -->

The model object holds everything the file defined.

> **Python note.** `zip(names, values)` pairs the two lists element by element, and `dict(...)` turns the pairs
> into a dictionary.

```{python}
print("Variables: ", jlmp.symbols["variables"])
print("Shocks:    ", jlmp.symbols["shocks"])
print("Exogenous: ", jlmp.symbols["exogenous"])
print("Parameters:", dict(zip(jlmp.symbols["parameters"], jlmp.calibration["parameters"])))
print("Options:   ", jlmp.options)
```

<!-- cell -->

Finally, Snowdrop can count the roots of the linearized model, as we did by hand in Section G.4. The model has one
forward-looking variable, inflation `PDOT(+1)`, so it needs exactly one root larger than 1 in absolute value.

```{python}
roots, text = quietly(driver.findEigenValues, model=jlmp)
roots = np.sort(np.abs(roots))
print("Absolute values of the roots:", np.round(roots, 3))
print("Roots larger than 1:", int(np.sum(roots > 1)), "| forward-looking variables: 1")
```

The model has one unstable root and one jump variable: the Blanchard–Kahn condition holds, and the model has a
unique stable solution.

<!-- cell -->

## G.6 Your first model file: the AS/AD model of Chapter 13

The best first model is one you already know. Chapter 13 combines an AD curve (the IS curve plus the central
bank's rule $R_t-\bar{r}=\bar{m}(\pi_t-\bar{\pi})$) with an AS curve (the Phillips curve with adaptive
expectations):

$$\tilde{Y}_t=\bar{a}_t-\bar{b}\bar{m}\,(\pi_t-\bar{\pi}), \qquad (G.5)$$

$$\pi_t=\pi_{t-1}+\bar{\nu}\,\tilde{Y}_t+\bar{o}_t. \qquad (G.6)$$

$\tilde{Y}_t$ is the output gap and $\pi_t$ inflation, both in percent. The demand shock $\bar{a}_t$ and the
inflation shock $\bar{o}_t$ move the economy away from its steady state, where output is at potential and inflation
equals the target $\bar{\pi}$. We use Chapter 13's baseline: $\bar{\pi}=2$, $\bar{m}=0.5$, $\bar{b}=2$ and
$\bar{\nu}=1$. The model has no expected future values, only the past ($\pi_{t-1}$), so it is not a DSGE model,
but it is written, solved and simulated with exactly the same tools.

<!-- cell -->

### Writing the model file

The notebook command `%%writefile` saves the rest of a cell as a file. One name needs care: $\pi$ is a built-in
constant (3.14159…) in the algebra library that Snowdrop uses, so a variable called `pi` would clash with it. We
call inflation `infl`.

```{python}
%%writefile asad.yaml
name: The AS/AD model of Chapter 13

symbols:
   variables: [Ytil, infl]           # output gap and inflation, in percent
   shocks: [a, o]                    # demand shock and inflation shock
   parameters: [b, m, nu, infl_bar]  # IS slope, policy response, Phillips slope, inflation target

equations:
   - Ytil = a - b*m*(infl - infl_bar)        # the AD curve (G.5)
   - infl = infl(-1) + nu*Ytil + o           # the AS curve (G.6)

calibration:
   b: 2.0
   m: 0.5
   nu: 1.0
   infl_bar: 2.0
   Ytil: 0.0                         # starting values: the steady state
   infl: 2.0

labels:
   Ytil: "Output gap, %"
   infl: "Inflation, %"

options:
   T: 20
   periods: [1]
   shock_values: [[0.0, 2.0]]        # Event 1: an inflation shock o = 2 in period 1
```

<!-- cell -->

### Event 1: an inflation shock

`load_model` reads the file, and `simulate` solves the model and returns a table with one row per period. Period 0
holds the starting values.

```{python}
asad = load_model("asad.yaml", verbose=True)
event1 = simulate(asad)
event1.head(6).round(3)
```

<!-- cell -->

These are the numbers of Chapter 13: inflation jumps to 3 percent, output falls 1 percent below potential, and the
gap to the target halves every period. Snowdrop's `plot` draws every variable of a simulation in its own panel.

> **Python note.** `plot(...)` is Snowdrop's chart function. `show=False, save=False` tells it to return the
> charts instead of showing and saving them, so that `show(...)` can draw them in the book's colors. `figs[0]` is
> the first (here the only) chart.

```{python}
figs = plot(path_to_dir=WORK, data=event1.to_numpy(), variable_names=list(event1.columns),
            var_labels=asad.symbols["variables_labels"], header="Event 1: an inflation shock",
            sizes=(1, 2), figsize=(10, 4), show=False, save=False)
show(figs[0], "Snowdrop's chart of the inflation shock: inflation jumps to 3 percent and output falls 1 percent", snowdrop=True)
```

<!-- cell -->

### Snowdrop and Chapter 13 agree

Chapter 13 solved the model period by period with a formula: given last period's inflation, equations (G.5) and
(G.6) are two linear equations in this period's $\tilde{Y}_t$ and $\pi_t$, with the solution
$\tilde{Y}_t=[\bar{a}_t-\bar{b}\bar{m}(\pi_{t-1}+\bar{o}_t-\bar{\pi})]/(1+\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})$. Here is that
solution again, to check Snowdrop against it.

```{python}
def ch13_path(a_list, o_list, infl_start=2.0, infl_bar=2.0, b=2.0, m=0.5, nu=1.0):
    """Chapter 13's solution of (G.5)-(G.6), one period at a time; period 0 is the starting point."""
    rows = [(0.0, infl_start)]
    for t in range(len(a_list)):
        infl_prev = rows[-1][1]
        Y = (a_list[t] - b * m * (infl_prev + o_list[t] - infl_bar)) / (1 + b * m * nu)
        rows.append((Y, infl_prev + nu * Y + o_list[t]))
    return pd.DataFrame(rows, columns=["Ytil", "infl"])

no_shock = [0.0] * 20
check1 = ch13_path(no_shock, [2.0] + [0.0] * 19)
gap = event1.to_numpy() - check1.iloc[:len(event1)].to_numpy()   # same periods
print(f"Largest difference between Snowdrop and Chapter 13: {np.abs(gap).max():.1e}")
```

> **Python note.** `[0.0] * 20` repeats the list: twenty zeros. `[2.0] + [0.0] * 19` joins two lists: a shock of 2
> in period 1 and zeros afterwards.

<!-- cell -->

### Event 2: disinflation

The central bank lowers its inflation target from 4 to 2 percent. We start the economy at the old steady state,
with inflation at 4 percent, and use the new target of 2 percent from period 1 on. No shock hits.

```{python}
asad = load_model("asad.yaml")
set_values(asad, "variables", {"infl": 4.0})          # inflation starts at the old target
asad.options["shock_values"] = [[0.0, 0.0]]           # no shock
event2 = simulate(asad)
figs = plot(path_to_dir=WORK, data=event2.to_numpy(), variable_names=list(event2.columns),
            var_labels=asad.symbols["variables_labels"], header="Event 2: disinflation from 4 to 2 percent",
            sizes=(1, 2), figsize=(10, 4), show=False, save=False)
show(figs[0], "Disinflation: a recession of 1 percent brings inflation from 4 down to 2 percent", snowdrop=True)

check2 = ch13_path(no_shock, no_shock, infl_start=4.0)
print(f"Largest difference to Chapter 13: {np.abs(event2.to_numpy() - check2.iloc[:len(event2)].to_numpy()).max():.1e}")
```

<!-- cell -->

### Event 3: a positive demand shock

Spending rises by $\bar{a}=2$ percent of potential output for nine periods, then returns to normal. A shock that
lasts several periods is a list of periods with one row of shock values for each.

```{python}
asad = load_model("asad.yaml")
asad.options["periods"] = list(range(1, 10))          # periods 1, 2, ..., 9
asad.options["shock_values"] = [[2.0, 0.0]] * 9      # a = 2 and o = 0 in each of them
event3 = simulate(asad)
figs = plot(path_to_dir=WORK, data=event3.to_numpy(), variable_names=list(event3.columns),
            var_labels=asad.symbols["variables_labels"], header="Event 3: a demand shock in periods 1-9",
            sizes=(1, 2), figsize=(10, 4), show=False, save=False)
show(figs[0], "A demand shock: output booms, inflation climbs toward 4 percent, then a recession follows", snowdrop=True)

check3 = ch13_path([2.0] * 9 + [0.0] * 11, no_shock)
print(f"Largest difference to Chapter 13: {np.abs(event3.to_numpy() - check3.iloc[:len(event3)].to_numpy()).max():.1e}")
```

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.** All three events reproduce Chapter 13 exactly. The demand shock first raises output and
inflation; as inflation rises, the central bank's rule raises the real interest rate and pulls output back to
potential, with inflation stuck near 4 percent. When the shock ends, the economy needs a recession to bring
inflation back to 2 percent.

<!-- cell -->

**Your turn.** Make monetary policy more aggressive, $\bar{m}=1$, and rerun Event 1. By how much does output fall
in period 1, and how fast does the inflation gap close? (Chapter 13: each period the gap shrinks by the factor
$\lambda=1/(1+\bar{b}\bar{m}\bar{\nu})$.)

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

With $\bar{m}=1$, $\lambda=1/3$: the inflation gap falls to a third each period instead of a half, and output falls
by $\bar{b}\bar{m}\lambda\bar{o}=2\times1\times\tfrac{1}{3}\times2\approx1.33$ percent in period 1, more than the
1 percent of the baseline. A tougher central bank buys faster disinflation with a deeper first recession.

```python
asad = load_model("asad.yaml")
set_values(asad, "parameters", {"m": 1.0})
simulate(asad).head(5).round(3)
```

</details>

## G.7 The paper's example: a monetary policy model with expectations

<!-- cell -->

### The model, read as economics

The paper's model has four equations. In the file, `PDOT` is inflation $\pi_t$, `Y` the output gap $y_t$, `RS` the
central bank's interest rate $i_t$ and `RR` the real interest rate $r_t$. All four are deviations from the steady
state, in decimals (0.01 is one percentage point). With the paper's names for the parameters:

$$\pi_t = p_1\,\pi_{t+1} + (1-p_1)\,\pi_{t-1} + p_2\Big(\frac{g^2}{g-y_t}-g\Big) + p_3\Big(\frac{g^2}{g-y_{t-1}}-g\Big) + \varepsilon^{\pi}_t, \qquad (G.7)$$

$$r_t = i_t - p_1\,\pi_{t+1} - (1-p_1)\,\pi_{t-1} + \varepsilon^{r}_t, \qquad (G.8)$$

$$i_t = p_4\,\pi_t + y_t + \varepsilon^{i}_t + \text{exo}_t, \qquad (G.9)$$

$$y_t = p_5\,y_{t-1} - p_6\,r_t - p_7\,r_{t-1} + \varepsilon^{y}_t. \qquad (G.10)$$

- (G.7) is a **Phillips curve** that mixes expected inflation (weight $p_1=0.414$) and past inflation. The output
  gap enters through $g^2/(g-y)-g$, which is close to $y$ when the gap is small but rises ever faster as $y$
  approaches $g=0.049$: an economy near full capacity sees inflation accelerate. Booms raise inflation by more
  than slumps of the same size lower it. Such a **convex** Phillips curve was a feature of the IMF's models of the
  1990s.
- (G.8) defines the **real interest rate**: the policy rate minus the inflation people expect (Chapters 8 and 12).
- (G.9) is the **policy rule**: the rate rises by $p_4=3$ points for each point of inflation and one for one with
  the output gap. $\text{exo}_t$ is a deliberate change of policy, set from outside.
- (G.10) is an **IS curve** with lags: a higher real interest rate, now or last period, lowers the output gap
  (Chapters 11 and 12).

Because inflation and the real rate depend on expected inflation, the model is forward-looking; because of the
convex term, it is nonlinear.

<!-- cell -->

```{python}
g = 0.049
y_gap = np.linspace(-0.04, 0.03, 141)
fig, ax = book_figure()
ax.plot(100 * y_gap, 100 * y_gap, color=GRAY, linestyle="--", label="a linear Phillips curve: $y$")
ax.plot(100 * y_gap, 100 * (g**2 / (g - y_gap) - g), color=BLUE, label="the paper's term: $g^2/(g-y)-g$")
ax.set_title("The output gap enters the Phillips curve in a convex way")
ax.set_xlabel("output gap $y$, percent")
ax.set_ylabel("effect on inflation, before $p_2$")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
show(fig, "The convex term equals the gap near zero but rises much faster for large positive gaps")
```

<!-- cell -->

### The paper's listing and the package's file

The file you printed in Section G.5 is not quite the listing in the paper. The differences are harmless, but you
need to know them to reproduce the paper:

| | The paper's listing | Snowdrop's `JLMP98.yaml` |
|---|---|---|
| Parameter names | `p1`, …, `p7` | `p_pdot1`, `p_pdot2`, `p_pdot3`, `p_rs1`, `p_y1`, `p_y2`, `p_y3` |
| Shocks | one, `ey` (to output) | four: `ey`, `err`, `ers`, `epdot` (one per equation) |
| Layout | `equations` and `calibration` indented under `symbols` (a slip: Snowdrop would reject it) | separate blocks |
| The policy revision | `exo: [0,0,0,0.03,0]` in `calibration` | not set; we set it below |
| Shock | `periods: [1]`, `shock_values: [std]` with `std: 0.02` | the same |

<!-- cell -->

### Solving with Newton's method

Snowdrop solves nonlinear models along the whole path, as in Section G.4: it stacks the four equations for every
period and applies Newton's method until the residuals vanish. First the output shock alone, with both of
Snowdrop's methods. `quietly` keeps Snowdrop's report, and we print its last lines.

```{python}
paths = {}
for method in ["LBJ", "ABLR"]:
    jlmp = load_model("JLMP98.yaml", Solver=method)
    jlmp.options["periods"] = [1]
    jlmp.options["shock_values"] = [0.02]             # ey = 0.02: a 2 percent output shock in period 1
    (y, dates), text = quietly(driver.run, model=jlmp, Plot=False)
    paths[method] = np.asarray(y)
    print(method, "|", " | ".join(text.strip().splitlines()[-2:]))

print(f"Largest difference between the two methods: {np.abs(paths['LBJ'] - paths['ABLR']).max():.1e}")
```

<!-- cell -->

Newton's method needs a handful of iterations because the model is nonlinear, and the two methods find the same
path.

<!-- cell -->

### Replicating the paper's Fig. 1

The paper adds a revision of monetary policy: in period 4 the policy rate is raised by 3 percentage points on top of
what the rule says, for one period. That is a path for the exogenous variable `exo`: 0.03 in period 4 and 0 from
period 5 on. `getExogenousSeries` turns the path into the form Snowdrop uses.

> **Python note.** `pd.Series([0.03, 0.0], index=[4, 5])` is a column of two numbers labelled by the periods 4
> and 5. Snowdrop keeps the last value for all later periods.

```{python}
from snowdrop.src.utils.util import getExogenousSeries

jlmp = load_model("JLMP98.yaml", Solver="LBJ")
jlmp.options["periods"] = [1]
jlmp.options["shock_values"] = [0.02]                 # the 2 percent output shock in period 1
jlmp.symbolic.exog_data = {"exo": pd.Series([0.03, 0.0], index=[4, 5])}
jlmp.calibration["exogenous"] = getExogenousSeries(jlmp)
fig1 = simulate(jlmp)
(100 * fig1.iloc[:9]).round(2)                       # in percent, periods 0 to 8
```

<!-- cell -->

Compare with the paper's Fig. 1: inflation rises to about 0.9 percent in period 1 and 1.1 percent in period 2, and
falls to about −0.45 percent in period 5; the real interest rate jumps to 4 percent; the output gap is 1.6
percent in period 1 and −0.9 percent in period 2. The table has the same numbers.

Before we trust a nonlinear solution, we check it: put the path back into the four equations and look at what is
left over.

```{python}
from snowdrop.src.numeric.solver.util import checkSolution

errors = checkSolution(jlmp, periods=jlmp.options["periods"], y=fig1.to_numpy())
print(f"LBJ: largest residual of the four equations: {np.abs(errors).max():.1e}")

jlmp_ablr = load_model("JLMP98.yaml", Solver="ABLR")
jlmp_ablr.options["periods"] = [1]
jlmp_ablr.options["shock_values"] = [0.02]
jlmp_ablr.symbolic.exog_data = {"exo": pd.Series([0.03, 0.0], index=[4, 5])}
jlmp_ablr.calibration["exogenous"] = getExogenousSeries(jlmp_ablr)
path_ablr = simulate(jlmp_ablr)
errors = checkSolution(jlmp_ablr, periods=jlmp_ablr.options["periods"], y=path_ablr.to_numpy())
print(f"ABLR: largest residual of the four equations: {np.abs(errors).max():.1e}")
```

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.** The LBJ path satisfies the equations to machine precision. The ABLR path leaves a residual of
exactly 0.03 in the policy rule: in this version of Snowdrop, the ABLR method does not apply the exogenous path,
although it solved the output shock alone correctly. Nothing in Snowdrop's report warns about it; only the residual
check reveals it. This is why the paper's model runs with LBJ, and why you should check residuals.

<!-- cell -->

Now the chart. `plotDecomposition` draws, for each variable, the **contribution** of each term on the right-hand
side of its equation, as stacked bars, with the total as a line.

```{python}
figs = plotDecomposition(path_to_dir=WORK, model=jlmp, y=fig1.to_numpy(), variables_names=list(fig1.columns),
                         decomp_variables=["PDOT", "RR", "RS", "Y"], periods=jlmp.options["periods"],
                         header="Shock to Output and Revision of Nominal Interest Rate", bPercent=True,
                         show=False, save=False)
show(figs[0], "Replication of Fig. 1 of the Snowdrop paper: contributions to inflation, the real and policy "
     "interest rates and the output gap", snowdrop=True)
```

<!-- cell -->

### Reading a contribution chart

Each panel splits one equation. For inflation, equation (G.7) says that inflation is the sum of five terms: the
lead of inflation, the lag of inflation, the output gap term, the lagged output gap term and the inflation shock.
In each period the bars show the size of each term, positive above zero and negative below, and they add up to the
black line. Snowdrop's `decompose` function returns the numbers behind the bars.

```{python}
from snowdrop.src.numeric.solver.util import decompose

T_fig = len(fig1)
parts, names = decompose(jlmp, fig1.to_numpy(), list(fig1.columns), "PDOT", T_fig, jlmp.options["periods"], False)
parts = 100 * pd.DataFrame(parts, index=fig1.index)  # in percent
parts["sum of the terms"] = parts.sum(axis=1)
parts["inflation"] = 100 * fig1["PDOT"]
parts.iloc[1:7].round(3)
```

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.** The terms add up to inflation. In period 1 the output shock opens a positive output gap, and
the output gap term pushes inflation up; so does the lead of inflation, because people expect the boom to raise
inflation next period too. The central bank's rule answers with a large rise of the policy rate, so the real
interest rate jumps to 4 percent and the output gap turns negative from period 2. Inflation peaks in period 2,
carried by its own lag and the lagged boom, and is below zero by period 4. The policy revision in period 4 raises
the real interest rate once more and deepens the slump in period 5, when inflation reaches its low of about −0.46
percent. The paper's chart tells this whole story at a glance.

## G.8 A real business cycle model

<!-- cell -->

### The model

Chapter 15 described real business cycle (RBC) models: an economy without frictions, hit by productivity shocks.
Snowdrop's `RBC.yaml` is the simplest one with a household that chooses how much to save. Labor is fixed at one.

$$\frac{1}{C_t}=\beta\,\frac{1+r_t}{C_{t+1}} \qquad (G.11)$$

$$Y_t = C_t + K_t-(1-\delta)K_{t-1} \qquad (G.12)$$

$$Y_t = K_{t-1}^{\gamma}\,A_t^{1-\gamma} \qquad (G.13)$$

$$\gamma\,\frac{Y_{t+1}}{K_t}=r_t+\delta \qquad (G.14)$$

$$\log A_t=\rho\log A_{t-1}+(1-\rho)\log a+\varepsilon_t \qquad (G.15)$$

- (G.11) is the **Euler equation** of Chapter 16 with log utility: the household gives up a unit of consumption
  today if the return $1+r_t$, discounted by $\beta$, makes up for it.
- (G.12) is the **resource constraint**: output is consumed or invested, and investment $K_t-(1-\delta)K_{t-1}$
  builds the capital stock, which depreciates at rate $\delta$ (Chapter 17).
- (G.13) is the **production function** of Chapter 4, with labor-augmenting technology $A_t$.
- (G.14) says that capital is rented until its marginal product equals its user cost $r_t+\delta$ (Chapter 17).
  Capital chosen in period $t$ produces in $t+1$.
- (G.15) is the **technology shock**, an AR(1) in logs around the level $a$.

The calibration is $\beta=0.99$, $\gamma=0.5$, $\delta=0.03$, $\rho=0.8$ and $a=0.1$, with one period a quarter.

```{python}
print(open("RBC.yaml").read())
```

<!-- cell -->

### The steady state by hand

In the steady state nothing changes, so (G.11) gives $1=\beta(1+r)$, (G.14) gives the capital–output ratio, and
(G.13) and (G.12) give output and consumption:

$$r^*=\frac{1}{\beta}-1,\qquad \frac{K^*}{Y^*}=\frac{\gamma}{r^*+\delta},\qquad Y^*=a\Big(\frac{K^*}{Y^*}\Big)^{\gamma/(1-\gamma)},\qquad C^*=Y^*-\delta K^*. \qquad (G.16)$$

The third formula comes from writing (G.13) as $Y=(K/Y)^{\gamma/(1-\gamma)}A$ with $A=a$.

```{python}
beta, gamma, delta, a_level = 0.99, 0.5, 0.03, 0.1
r_star = 1 / beta - 1
KY = gamma / (r_star + delta)
Y_star = a_level * KY ** (gamma / (1 - gamma))
K_star = KY * Y_star
C_star = Y_star - delta * K_star
steady = {"K": K_star, "r": r_star, "A": a_level, "Y": Y_star, "C": C_star}
pd.Series(steady).round(5)
```

<!-- cell -->

Snowdrop has a steady-state solver. It starts from the starting values in the file and searches with Newton's
method.

```{python}
rbc = load_model("RBC.yaml")
(ss, growth), text = quietly(driver.findSteadyStateSolution, model=rbc)
comparison = pd.DataFrame({"by hand": pd.Series(steady), "Snowdrop": pd.Series(ss, index=rbc.symbols["variables"])})
comparison["difference, %"] = 100 * (comparison["Snowdrop"] / comparison["by hand"] - 1)
comparison.round(5)
```

<!-- cell -->

Snowdrop's answer is close, but its capital stock is about 0.3 percent too high. Its search stops with residuals
of about 0.00003, which it treats as small enough. For dynamic simulations that is not quite good enough: a model
that starts slightly off its steady state drifts even when no shock hits. When the steady state has a formula, use
the formula. We put the exact values in as starting values, and check: the steady-state solver now returns them
unchanged, and a simulation with no shock stays put.

```{python}
rbc = load_model("RBC.yaml")
set_values(rbc, "variables", steady)
(ss, growth), text = quietly(driver.findSteadyStateSolution, model=rbc)
print("Snowdrop's steady state, starting from the formula:", np.round(ss, 5))

rbc.options["shock_values"] = [[0.0]]                 # no shock
calm = simulate(rbc)
print(f"With no shock, the largest move away from the steady state: {np.abs(calm - calm.iloc[0]).to_numpy().max():.1e}")
```

<!-- cell -->

### A technology shock under perfect foresight

The file's experiment is a technology shock $\varepsilon_1=0.1$ in period 1: technology jumps 10.5 percent and then
returns to its steady state at the rate $\rho=0.8$. After the shock, households and firms know the future path of
technology: the solution is a **perfect-foresight** path, found with Newton's method as before.

```{python}
rbc = load_model("RBC.yaml")
set_values(rbc, "variables", steady)                  # start from the exact steady state
tfp = simulate(rbc)                                   # the file's shock: 0.1 in period 1
rbc_labels = {"K": "Capital", "r": "Interest rate (quarterly)", "A": "Technology", "Y": "Output", "C": "Consumption"}
figs = plot(path_to_dir=WORK, data=tfp.iloc[:61].to_numpy(), variable_names=list(tfp.columns), var_labels=rbc_labels,
            header="A technology shock in the RBC model (60 quarters)", sizes=(2, 3), figsize=(12, 6.5),
            show=False, save=False)
show(figs[0], "Snowdrop's chart of the RBC model after a technology shock: capital, the interest rate, "
     "technology, output and consumption", snowdrop=True)
```

<!-- cell -->

The levels hide the sizes. **Impulse responses** show each variable as a percent deviation from its steady state
(the interest rate in percentage points, at an annual rate).

```{python}
irf = 100 * (tfp / pd.Series(steady) - 1)            # percent deviations from the steady state
irf["r"] = 400 * (tfp["r"] - r_star)                 # percentage points, annual rate
irf = irf[["A", "Y", "C", "K", "r"]]
irf.iloc[[1, 2, 4, 8, 16, 40]].round(2)
```

<!-- cell -->

```{python}
fig, ax = book_figure()
labels = {"Y": "output", "C": "consumption", "K": "capital", "A": "technology"}
colors = {"Y": BLUE, "C": TEAL, "K": GREEN, "A": GRAY}
for name in ["A", "Y", "C", "K"]:
    style = "--" if name == "A" else "-"
    ax.plot(irf.index[:41], irf[name].iloc[:41], color=colors[name], linestyle=style, label=labels[name])
ax.axhline(0, color=AXIS, linewidth=1, gid="rule")
ax.set_title("Impulse responses to a technology shock of 10 percent")
ax.set_xlabel("quarters after the shock")
ax.set_ylabel("percent deviation from the steady state")
ax.legend()
show(fig, "Output jumps with technology; consumption rises little but stays up; capital builds up slowly")
```

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.** Output jumps with technology, by about half as much (the exponent $1-\gamma=0.5$ in (G.13)).
Consumption rises only a little: the household knows the shock is temporary and smooths consumption (Chapter 16).
The rest of the extra output is invested, so capital builds up for several years, and it keeps output and
consumption above their steady state after technology has returned to normal. The interest rate rises with the
marginal product of capital and then falls below its steady state while the extra capital is run down.

<!-- cell -->

### How nonlinear is the model?

The RBC model is nonlinear: (G.13) has a power, (G.11) a ratio. Linear solution methods, like Klein's and Dynare's
first-order perturbation, replace the model by a straight-line approximation around the steady state. A linear model
responds in proportion to the shock: twice the shock, twice the response. We can test how far the RBC model is from
that. We simulate technology shocks $\varepsilon_1$ of 0.01, 0.1, 0.3 and −0.3 (in logs, so roughly 1, 10, 30 and
−30 percent) and scale each response of output to a shock of 1 percent.

```{python}
fig, ax = book_figure()
sizes = [0.01, 0.1, 0.3, -0.3]
colors = [GRAY, BLUE, TEAL, RUST]
for k in range(len(sizes)):
    rbc = load_model("RBC.yaml")
    set_values(rbc, "variables", steady)
    rbc.options["shock_values"] = [[sizes[k]]]
    path = simulate(rbc)
    per_unit = 100 * (path["Y"] / Y_star - 1) / (100 * sizes[k])   # % response per 1% shock
    ax.plot(per_unit.index[:41], per_unit.iloc[:41], color=colors[k], label=f"shock of {100 * sizes[k]:+.0f}%")
ax.set_title("Output response per 1 percent of shock, for four shock sizes")
ax.set_xlabel("quarters after the shock")
ax.set_ylabel("percent per percent of shock")
ax.legend()
show(fig, "The responses to small shocks coincide; large positive and negative shocks give different responses per unit")
```

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.** For small shocks the scaled responses lie on top of each other, so a linear solution would be
accurate. For shocks of ±30 percent they come apart: per unit of shock, a large positive shock raises output by
more than a large negative one lowers it. Technology enters in logs, so $\varepsilon=0.3$ raises $A$ by 35 percent
($e^{0.3}-1$), while $\varepsilon=-0.3$ lowers it by only 26 percent. Normal business cycles are small, so linear methods serve well for estimation
(Sections G.11 and G.12). Big events (a pandemic, a financial crisis) are where nonlinear methods like Snowdrop's
earn their keep.

<!-- cell -->

### Random shocks: one model, many histories

So far one shock hit, once. In `RBC1.yaml`, two shocks hit every period: the technology shock and a shock to output
in (G.13). They are drawn from a normal distribution (`!MvNormal`) for ten different histories (`Npaths`). The file
gives the shocks means of −0.05 and 0.05; we set both to zero, so that the shocks only add noise around the steady
state.

```{python}
text = open("RBC1.yaml").read().replace("mean: [-0.05,0.05]", "mean: [0.0, 0.0]")
open("RBC1_zero.yaml", "w").write(text)
print(text[text.find("options"):])
```

<!-- cell -->

> **Python note.** `np.random.seed(2026)` fixes the random numbers, so that the same histories come out every
> time the notebook runs. A stochastic run returns an array with three dimensions: path, period and variable.

One more setting matters. By default, Snowdrop solves each history as one perfect-foresight path: it imposes all
the random shocks at once, as if households knew in period 1 every shock still to come. In a stochastic simulation
the shocks must be **surprises**. `anticipate=False` makes Snowdrop solve the model period by period and reveal each
shock only when it hits. This takes a few seconds longer.

```{python}
rbc1 = load_model("RBC1_zero.yaml", anticipate=False)
set_values(rbc1, "variables", steady)
np.random.seed(2026)
(y, dates), text = quietly(driver.run, model=rbc1, Plot=False, anticipate=False)
print("Shape of the result (paths, periods, variables):", np.shape(y))
figs = plot(path_to_dir=WORK, data=np.asarray(y), variable_names=rbc1.symbols["variables"], Npaths=10,
            var_labels=rbc_labels, header="Ten histories of the RBC model with random shocks", sizes=(2, 3), figsize=(12, 6.5),
            show=False, save=False)
show(figs[0], "Ten simulated histories of output, consumption, capital, the interest rate and technology", snowdrop=True)
```

<!-- cell -->

**What to notice.** The same model, the same parameters and the same distribution of shocks produce ten different
histories. This is how DSGE models see the business cycle: a stable economy constantly hit by small random shocks.
Consumption is much smoother than output in every history, and capital moves slowly around its steady state. (Run
the cell without `anticipate=False` and you will see what goes wrong when households know the future: consumption
jumps once in period 1 and then drifts, and capital wanders far from its steady state.) Estimation (Sections G.11 and
G.12) asks the reverse question: given one observed history, which parameters make it most likely?

<!-- cell -->

**Your turn.** Make technology shocks more persistent, $\rho=0.95$, and draw the impulse responses again. How does
the response of consumption change, and why?

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

A more persistent shock raises income for longer, so it is closer to a permanent rise in income: consumption jumps
by more on impact (the permanent income idea of Chapter 16), and the household invests less of each extra unit of
output.

set_values(rbc, "parameters", {"rho": 0.95})
set_values(rbc, "variables", steady)          # the steady state does not depend on rho

(100 * (path / pd.Series(steady) - 1))[["A", "Y", "C", "K"]].iloc[[1, 4, 8, 20]].round(2)

## G.9 From model to data: state space and the Kalman filter

<!-- cell -->

### The solved model is a state-space model

Once a linear model is solved, its decision rules say how the variables today depend on the variables yesterday and
on today's shocks. Stack the variables into a vector $s_t$, the **state**:

$$s_t = T\,s_{t-1} + R\,\varepsilon_t \qquad \text{(transition equation)}$$

$$y_t = Z\,s_t + u_t \qquad \text{(measurement equation)}$$

The first line is the model. The second says which combinations of the state we **observe** in the data, $y_t$,
perhaps with measurement errors $u_t$. In Ireland's model of Section G.11 the state has seven variables and the
data three. The output gap, the preference shock and the cost-push shock are never observed. The **Kalman filter**
does two jobs at once: it infers the unobserved states from the data, period by period, and it computes the
**likelihood** of the data, the number that estimation maximizes. We build it for the smallest case first.

<!-- cell -->

### A Kalman filter for one variable

The state is an AR(1), and we observe it with noise:

$$s_t=\rho\,s_{t-1}+e_t,\quad e_t\sim N(0,\sigma_e^2), \qquad (G.17)$$

$$y_t=s_t+u_t,\quad u_t\sim N(0,\sigma_u^2). \qquad (G.18)$$

Think of $s_t$ as the true output gap and $y_t$ as a noisy first estimate of it. We simulate 200 periods with
$\rho=0.9$ and $\sigma_e=\sigma_u=1$, so we know the truth and can see how well the filter recovers it.

> **Python note.** `np.random.default_rng(2026)` creates a random number generator with a fixed seed, so the
> numbers are the same every time; `rng.normal()` draws one number from the standard normal distribution.

```{python}
rho_true, sig_e, sig_u = 0.9, 1.0, 1.0
T_data = 200
rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
s_true = np.zeros(T_data)
y_obs = np.zeros(T_data)
s_prev = 0.0
for t in range(T_data):
    s_true[t] = rho_true * s_prev + sig_e * rng.normal()    # equation (G.17)
    y_obs[t] = s_true[t] + sig_u * rng.normal()             # equation (G.18)
    s_prev = s_true[t]
print(f"Standard deviation of the state: {s_true.std():.2f}, of the data: {y_obs.std():.2f}")
```

<!-- cell -->

Each period the filter does three things. Write $\hat{s}_{t|t-1}$ for the best guess of the state before seeing
$y_t$, $\hat{s}_{t|t}$ for the guess after, and $P$ for the variance (the uncertainty) of each guess.

1. **Predict** the state with the model: $\hat{s}_{t|t-1}=\rho\,\hat{s}_{t-1|t-1}$ and
   $P_{t|t-1}=\rho^2P_{t-1|t-1}+\sigma_e^2$. (G.19)
2. **Compare** with the data: the forecast error is $v_t=y_t-\hat{s}_{t|t-1}$, with variance
   $F_t=P_{t|t-1}+\sigma_u^2$. (G.20)
3. **Update**: move the guess toward the data by the **Kalman gain** $K_t=P_{t|t-1}/F_t$:
   $\hat{s}_{t|t}=\hat{s}_{t|t-1}+K_tv_t$ and $P_{t|t}=(1-K_t)P_{t|t-1}$. (G.21)

The gain weighs the two sources of information: when the model's prediction is uncertain ($P$ large) the filter
trusts the data; when the data are noisy ($\sigma_u$ large) it trusts the model. Before the first observation we use
the long-run variance of the state, $\sigma_e^2/(1-\rho^2)$; Snowdrop calls this choice `Prior="Equilibrium"`.

**The likelihood comes for free.** If the model is right, each forecast error $v_t$ is normal with mean 0 and
variance $F_t$. The probability of the whole sample is the product of these normal densities, so its logarithm is
a sum:

$$\log L=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{t=1}^{T}\Big(\log 2\pi+\log F_t+\frac{v_t^2}{F_t}\Big). \qquad (G.22)$$

```{python}
def kalman_filter(y, rho, sig_e, sig_u):
    """Equations (G.19)-(G.21) for the model (G.17)-(G.18); returns the filtered states and log L of (G.22)."""
    s_hat = 0.0                                    # the state's mean before any data
    P = sig_e**2 / (1 - rho**2)                    # and its long-run variance
    filtered = np.zeros(len(y))
    loglik = 0.0
    for t in range(len(y)):
        s_pred = rho * s_hat                       # 1. predict
        P_pred = rho**2 * P + sig_e**2
        v = y[t] - s_pred                          # 2. compare: forecast error and its variance
        F = P_pred + sig_u**2
        K = P_pred / F                             # 3. update with the Kalman gain
        s_hat = s_pred + K * v
        P = (1 - K) * P_pred
        filtered[t] = s_hat
        loglik = loglik - 0.5 * (np.log(2 * np.pi) + np.log(F) + v**2 / F)
    return filtered, loglik

filtered, loglik = kalman_filter(y_obs, rho_true, sig_e, sig_u)
print(f"Log-likelihood at the true parameters: {loglik:.2f}")
print(f"Typical error: data {np.std(y_obs - s_true):.2f}, filtered state {np.std(filtered - s_true):.2f}")
```

<!-- cell -->

```{python}
fig, ax = book_figure()
periods = np.arange(1, 81)
ax.plot(periods, y_obs[:80], color=GRAY, linestyle="none", marker="o", markersize=3.5, label="data $y_t$")
ax.plot(periods, s_true[:80], color=TEAL, linewidth=1.6, label="true state $s_t$")
ax.plot(periods, filtered[:80], color=BLUE, linewidth=2.4, label="filtered state $\\hat{s}_{t|t}$")
ax.set_title("The Kalman filter recovers the state from noisy data (first 80 periods)")
ax.set_xlabel("period")
ax.legend(loc="upper left")
show(fig, "The filtered state follows the true state much more closely than the noisy data do")
```

**What to notice.** The data jump around the true state; the filtered state follows the truth much more closely,
because it combines each new observation with what the model predicted. The filter's error is smaller than the
error of the raw data.

<!-- cell -->

**The same filter with matrices.** For a model with many variables, the scalars become matrices:
$P_{t|t-1}=TP_{t-1|t-1}T'+RQR'$, $F_t=ZP_{t|t-1}Z'+H$ and $K_t=P_{t|t-1}Z'F_t^{-1}$, where $Q$ and $H$ hold the
variances of the shocks and of the measurement errors. The log-likelihood has the same form, with $\log\det F_t$
and $v_t'F_t^{-1}v_t$. Snowdrop's `Durbin_Koopman` filter does this, in a version that is fast and numerically
careful (Durbin and Koopman, 2012).

<!-- cell -->

**Your turn.** Make the data noisier, $\sigma_u=3$: simulate the data again and filter them. How does the filtered
state change? Print the Kalman gain of the last period.

<details><summary>Show the answer</summary>

With noisy data the filter trusts the model more: the Kalman gain falls from about 0.6 to about 0.23, so each new
observation moves the estimate less. The filtered state becomes smoother and reacts to the data more slowly.

```python
sig_u = 3.0
y_noisy = s_true + sig_u * np.random.default_rng(7).normal(size=T_data)
filtered_noisy, ll = kalman_filter(y_noisy, rho_true, sig_e, sig_u)
P = sig_e**2 / (1 - rho_true**2)
for t in range(T_data):                       # the gain does not depend on the data, only on the variances
    P_pred = rho_true**2 * P + sig_e**2
    K = P_pred / (P_pred + sig_u**2)
    P = (1 - K) * P_pred
print(f"Kalman gain with sig_u = 3: {K:.2f}")
sig_u = 1.0                                   # back to the baseline
```
